title: Stories Are Weapons: Psychological Warfare and the American Mind
description:
A history of psychological warfare in the United States and of how its methods moved from foreign campaigns into domestic culture wars, by the journalist and novelist Annalee Newitz.

Newitz begins with Benjamin Franklin's fake newspaper in the Revolutionary War and the nineteenth-century wars on Indigenous nations, and follows the line through the Cold War to online influence campaigns. The book argues that postwar psychological operatives drew on science fiction writing and advertising, and that these tactics now appear in fights over race and intelligence, school boards and LGBT students, and feminism. It closes on researchers and activists working toward what Newitz calls psychological disarmament. Norton published the hardcover on 4 June 2024.

Newitz is a science journalist who also writes fiction, and was the founder of io9 and editor-in-chief of Gizmodo. Earlier nonfiction includes Four Lost Cities and Scatter, Adapt, and Remember. Their novels include Autonomous, The Future of Another Timeline and The Terraformers.

title: Obfuscation: A User's Guide for Privacy and Protest
description:
A handbook for resisting data collection by adding noise to it, written for ordinary users who cannot opt out of surveillance by corporations and governments.

Brunton and Nissenbaum define obfuscation as the deliberate use of ambiguous, confusing or misleading information to interfere with surveillance. They draw on cases from radar chaff dropped by Second World War pilots to Twitter bots that disrupted protest hashtags and software that masks search queries, then ask whether such tactics are justified and how they can be combined with other privacy practices and tools. The MIT Press edition was published in September 2015.

When the book appeared, Finn Brunton taught media, culture and communication at New York University, and Helen Nissenbaum was a professor there and directed its Information Law Institute. Brunton is also the author of Spam: A Shadow History of the Internet.

title: Through the Crosshairs: War, Visual Culture, and the Weaponized Gaze
description:
A study of how footage from weapon-mounted cameras left the battlefield and became a familiar part of civilian screen culture.

Stahl follows gun-camera and targeting imagery through news broadcasts, entertainment, video games and social media. He argues that this view through the crosshairs shapes how the public understands armed conflict and state violence. The book appeared from Rutgers University Press in June 2018 in its War Culture series.

Roger Stahl is an associate professor of communication studies at the University of Georgia. He wrote Militainment, Inc. and has worked on documentary films about the relationship between the military and entertainment industries, including Returning Fire. This book carries that research from entertainment into the imagery of surveillance and targeting.

title: No Place to Hide: Behind the Scenes of Our Emerging Surveillance Society
description:
An investigative account of how private data brokers and government agencies built a shared system for tracking Americans after September 11.

O'Harrow follows companies such as Acxiom, ChoicePoint and Seisint, which hold billions of records on individuals and sell or share them with law enforcement and intelligence agencies. He names the result a "security industrial complex" and describes systems like the Matrix, which joined criminal records to commercial data. He also raises problems of inaccurate data and identity theft. Free Press published the book in 2005.

O'Harrow was a reporter for The Washington Post and a Pulitzer Prize finalist for articles on privacy and technology. He received the 2003 Carnegie Mellon Cyber Security Reporting Award. The book comes from his reporting on privacy and technology.

title: Black Transparency: The Right to Know in the Age of Mass Surveillance
description:
A book-length essay on involuntary disclosure, leaks and whistleblowing, written by a design studio rather than a policy analyst.

Metahaven uses the term black transparency for information that escapes against the will of its keepers, and follows it through international relations, the ethics of whistleblowers and the surveillance of everyday digital life. The book mixes essay and fanzine formats, and ties transparency to design, architecture and popular culture. Sternberg Press published it in October 2015 in its Design series.

Metahaven is Vinca Kruk and Daniel van der Velden, who founded the studio in 2007. Its work includes the visual identity for WikiLeaks and the book Uncorporate Identity (2010).

title: Networks of New York: An Illustrated Field Guide to Urban Internet Infrastructure
description:
A pocket field guide to the physical internet, which Ingrid Burrington locates in the sidewalk markings, manhole covers and buildings of New York.

Burrington uses New York as her reference point and more than fifty color illustrations as her map. She decodes spray-painted sidewalk markings, explains the history behind cryptic manhole covers, and points out subway cameras and carrier hotels. Along the way she covers the NYPD's surveillance apparatus, twentieth-century telecommunication monopolies, high-frequency trading on Wall Street and the downtown building that houses both Google and the FBI's Joint Terrorism Task Force. Melville House published it in August 2016.

Burrington is a writer and artist based in Brooklyn whose work concerns data, internet infrastructure and the tech industry. She turned to network infrastructure in 2013, following the Snowden revelations. She is a founding member of Deep Lab, and her writing has appeared in The Atlantic and The Nation.

title: Before and After: Documenting the Architecture of Disaster
description:
A short illustrated essay on the before-and-after image as a way of documenting destruction, from its origins to satellite surveillance.

Satellite photography shows the effects of war or climate change from the distance of orbit, but rarely the event itself. Eyal and Ines Weizman argue that an architectural expert is needed to fill that gap with a narrative. They trace the before-and-after image from nineteenth-century Paris to current satellite imagery, in which state militaries monitor civilians and humanitarian organisations monitor the militaries. Interpreting these images is never straightforward, and the essay asks who can see in higher resolution and who controls the size of the pixels. The book runs 70 pages and was published by Strelka Press in 2014.

Eyal Weizman, an architect born in Haifa in 1970, founded the agency Forensic Architecture in 2010 and directs it at Goldsmiths, University of London. His books include Hollow Land (2007) and Forensic Architecture: Violence at the Threshold of Detectability (2017).

title: Can Jokes Bring Down Governments? Memes, Design and Politics
description:
An essay by the Amsterdam design studio Metahaven on how protest works when the stated position of government is that there is no alternative.

The book starts from the question of how one dissents in that situation. It proposes that protest now has new strategies, beginning with the internet meme, and treats jokes as an open-source weapon of politics. The essay addresses the austerity politics of Europe and the forms of resistance against them. It was published by Strelka Press (listed as Strelka Institute), as an 82-page paperback in 2014. The cover is a red silhouette of a cat washing itself.

Metahaven was founded in 2007 by the graphic designers Vinca Kruk and Daniel van der Velden, and describes itself as a strategic graphic design agency. Its work spans publications and digital projects, including the visual identity for WikiLeaks, the Sealand Identity Project and the books Uncorporate Identity (2010) and Black Transparency: The Right to Know in the Age of Mass Surveillance (2015).

title: The Administration of Fear
description:
A book-length interview in which Paul Virilio argues that fear has become an everyday landscape and that states have a stake in managing it.

Virilio describes a world that is itself limited, saturated and manipulated, with stock-market crises, undifferentiated terrorism and lightning pandemics producing a stressful claustrophobia. He argues that globalization has eroded the prerogatives of states, which now have to convince citizens that they can ensure their physical safety, and are tempted to orchestrate fear as policy. The "propaganda of progress" and the illuminism of new technologies supply further vectors for fear by manufacturing frenzy and stupor. Virilio reads the 2007 economic catastrophe as capitalism accelerating, not collapsing. The conversation is with Bertrand Richard and was translated by Ames Hodges. Semiotext(e) published it on 24 February 2012 as number 10 in its Intervention Series.

Virilio (1932-2018) was a French urbanist and theorist best known for dromology, the study of the logic and impact of speed. His other books include Speed and Politics, War and Cinema: The Logistics of Perception, Bunker Archaeology and The Information Bomb.

title: Propaganda: The Formation of Men's Attitudes
description:
A foundational analysis of propaganda by the French philosopher Jacques Ellul, who treats it as a permanent condition of technological society and not as an occasional wartime tool.

Ellul approaches propaganda through both psychology and sociology. He sorts its techniques into categories, traces how modern technology carries them through a population, and argues that propaganda is a threat to democratic life. Vintage issued the English-language paperback on 12 January 1973. The Los Angeles Times called it a presentation of propaganda as the most serious threat to humanity in the modern world, and Kirkus Reviews described the analysis as brilliant, thoroughgoing and frightening.

Ellul (1912-1994) taught at the University of Bordeaux and was involved in the French Resistance during the Second World War. He wrote widely on technology and its social effects, and the cover of this edition names The Technological Society as his earlier book. He is also described as a Christian anarchist.

title: Branding Terror: The Logotypes and Iconography of Insurgent Groups and Terrorist Organizations
description:
A reference work that reads terrorist and insurgent organizations as brands, cataloguing the symbols they use to announce themselves.

The book has more than sixty entries. Each gives a short account of a group's ideology, leadership and methods, then analyses its visual identity: the symbolism, colours and typography of its logo and flag. It also carries a chronology of major terrorist actions, a glossary, seven maps and about 150 colour illustrations. The authors state that it makes no political statements, and offer it as counter-intelligence insight and as a resource for graphic designers. Merrell published it in April 2013.

Artur Beifuss formerly worked for the United Nations as a counter-terrorism analyst. Francesco Trivini Bellini is a graphic designer and creative director. Steven Heller, formerly art director at the New York Times, wrote the foreword.
